title: Latency taxonomy and UX heuristics (draft)
content:
Context / why this exists:
This is a personal scratchpad to capture a working taxonomy of latency types relevant to Redwood-hosted inference and a set of lightweight UX heuristics we can bake into the Console, SDKs, and default behaviors. Goal: make it easier for product/ux/engineering to reason about user-facing behaviour across latency bands and to provide predictable, low-effort fallbacks for customers.

Quick summary (one-liner):
Map concrete latency classes to UX patterns and cost/quality tradeoffs; surface these as presets and guidance in the Console and SDKs.

Taxonomy (rough) — operational + perceived
1) Perceived instant (0–150ms):
   - What it feels like: instant, no special UI needed.
   - Sources: local cache hits (prefix/KV), on-device routing, micro-batched fast GPUs.
   - UX heuristics: synchronous response, minimal skeleton, animate micro-feedback for inputs.

2) Near-instant / conversational latency (150–500ms):
   - Feels snappy for short turns.
   - Sources: warm contexts, model variant with lower latency, streaming enabled but short TTIs.
   - UX heuristics: streaming token-by-token, cursor/typing indicator, optimistic acknowledgements for user actions.

3) Noticeable (500ms–2s):
   - Users sense delay. Complex outputs may still be acceptable.
   - Sources: larger models, cold context, network RTT, queueing during peaks.
   - UX heuristics: show progress indicators, partial results (incremental synthesis), fallbacks to condensed answer if timeout reached.

4) Slow (2s–8s):
   - Friction for interactive flows; acceptable for batch tasks.
   - Sources: long-generation, multi-hop tool calls, cross-region routing.
   - UX heuristics: explain expected wait time, enable "background delivery" (notify when ready), allow cancellations and quick summary placeholder.

5) Deferred / async (>8s):
   - Treat as background job; user expects notification later.
   - UX heuristics: job queue UI, progress mail/notification, results archive, retry/fail states.

Technical latency components to instrument (suggested metrics):
- TTFB (time to first byte / token start)
- TTR (time to receive recommended chunk size / streaming throughput)
- KV/prefix cache hit ratio and latency
- Model load/warmup time per variant
- End-to-end percentiles (p50/p95/p99) by route and model
- User-facing completion duration (time from click -> first token visible)

UX primitives and patterns to standardize
- Progressive Answer: emit structured partials (title -> bullets -> details).
- Graceful degrade: swap to cheaper model variant providing a concise summary, then optionally expand later.
- Streaming vs batch toggle: default streaming for <2s expected responses, batch for expensive generations.
- Local optimistic echo: show predicted short responses immediately while final server tokens stream in.
- Background completion: give short summary immediately, push full result asynchronously.
- Cancellation & resume: allow user to cancel long runs and resume from last snapshot (session id).

Product ideas / Console UX hooks
- Latency Presets: "Instant", "Conversational", "Throughput-first", "Cheap background" mapped to kernel/config templates (batching/quantization/model variant).
- Per-route latency budget: UI slider (ms) -> YAML config auto-suggests model + batching + cache TTL.
- Live suggestion: detect rising p95 and show "Enable fallback variant" CTA.
- SDK helper: client-side function that picks optimistic UI pattern based on configured budget and current roundtrip measurement.

Sample user stories (for a light PRD)
- As a product builder, I can set a per-endpoint latency budget; the platform suggests a config that meets the budget with estimated cost impact. Acceptance: budget slider + suggested config + cost delta shown.
- As an end user, when a conversational request exceeds 2s, I see a concise placeholder answer and a note that full details will arrive shortly. Acceptance: placeholder visible <500ms, full content arrives later.
- As an SRE, I get Console alerts when p95 latency crosses threshold and a one-click enablement of model-fallback for affected routes. Acceptance: alert + fallback toggle.

Open questions / unknowns
- What are safe defaults for partial-answer integrity? (we must avoid hallucinations when emitting summaries)
- How to represent cost tradeoffs clearly to customers without exposing internal pricing noise?
- Does the SDK measure client-side RTT and feed it back for better routing decisions? Privacy concerns?
- Interaction with Private/Dedicated deployments — we need consistent UX but different control surfaces (customer-managed infra).

Next steps / action items (personal to-dos):
- Sync with SRE to validate available latency telemetry (p50/p95/p99 by route) — @Ava
- Prototype a Console slider -> config mapping (quick mock in Figma) — assignment: me
- Draft a short customer-facing help article: "Why your assistant sometimes returns a short answer first" — pair with comms
- Run quick SDK experiment: measure client-side TTFB and send anonymized telemetry to route router to evaluate improvements in routing decisions.

Rough sketch of Console copy for fallback CTA:
"High latency detected for route /chat. Try enabling a lower-latency model variant (saves ~60% latency at ~20% quality delta)."

Notes to self (misc):
- Keep distinction between perceived latency and raw server time in product copy.
- Consider a "latency simulator" in Console for customers to preview behavior under different budgets.
- Check legal for async notification patterns (GDPR/consent) before push-notify flows.

End of scratchpad.
